Lessons.Title: Graph and Answer
ExplanationParagraphs: Original 2021 Grade 3 Unit 8 Lesson 7 connects directly to the genuine class or school survey collected in Lesson 6. Use the authentic recorded category labels and counts; do not invent observations to claim source-task completion.

Warm-up Notice and Wonder: Graph (10 minutes). Observe the original published graph with the teacher and discuss observations and questions. Original image details are linked but have not been pixel-verified, so no unsupported specific values are inferred.

Activity 1 Draw a Scaled Bar Graph (20 minutes). In groups, use the real surveyed categories and totals from the prior lesson. Decide how many responses ONE GRID UNIT represents, use equally spaced steps, create a clear title, label both category and frequency axes, and draw each bar to the corresponding observed count. Check the maximum and minimum bars for consistency.

A sensible scale must suit the collected maximum: 1, 2, 5 or another consistent number of respondents per interval. If a real count is not a multiple of the interval, explain and draw accurately between tick marks rather than rounding responses away.

Activity 2 Ask and Answer Questions (20 minutes). Students WRITE questions from their own graphs: How many more students chose category A than B? How many fewer chose B than A? How many more chose A OR B together than C? Exchange graphs with a partner, answer their questions, and explain the addition/subtraction reasoning.

Teacher synthesis checks observed data provenance, bar height versus the selected scale, labels and a valid explanation of each one-step or two-step category comparison. Partner-authored questions, handwritten graphs and observed surveys stay teacher reviewed.

Separate ORIGINAL EDULYTICS FICTIONAL worked example, not the original survey: suppose Space=12, Animals=8, Weather=4. With TWO students per vertical step, bar heights are 6, 4 and 2 steps. Space has 4 more than Animals; Space OR Animals combined exceed Weather by 12+8-4=16. This is a rehearsal and never replaces authentic source data.

Original gated publisher Graph Question Cool-down is not inspected or copied. Source standalone Student Task PDF and the warm-up artwork pixels remain unverified; keep teacher-linked source and do not claim exact one-to-one artwork parity.

KeyConcepts.Title: A scaled bar graph
KeyConcepts.Definition: A graph that represents observed category counts using equal numeric intervals.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Choose a consistent unit per scale interval and label the categories, counts and title.
KeyConcepts.Example: Fictional 12 responses shown as 6 equal intervals of 2 each.

KeyConcepts.Title: One-step comparison
KeyConcepts.Definition: Compare two graph frequencies by subtraction.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Read values from the scale before subtracting; do not subtract the number of drawn tick marks.

KeyConcepts.Title: Two-step OR comparison
KeyConcepts.Definition: Combine counts from two different categories and compare that total with a third category.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Add both disjoint categories, then subtract the comparison category.

KeyConcepts.Title: Source-data integrity
KeyConcepts.Definition: Lesson 7 must use the observed survey data collected in Lesson 6 for the authentic source task.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Fictional example counts remain separately labeled; drawing and partner exchange require teacher review.
KeyConcepts.Example: Retain labels and original tallies from the previous lesson.

WorkedExamples.Title: Independently authored scaled bars and comparisons
WorkedExamples.Question: Fictional data: Space 12, Animals 8, Weather 4 students. Use a scale of 2 responses per interval. How tall is each bar, how many more chose Space than Animals, and how many more chose Space or Animals than Weather?
WorkedExamples.Method: Convert each count into graph intervals; read scale before 1- and 2-step comparisons.
Steps: Together Space or Animals = 12+8=20 students because responses use distinct categories.
WorkedExamples.Check: Read back bars 6x2=12, 4x2=8, 2x2=4. Check 12+8-4=16. Original school survey remains separate.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Bar height is treated as the count even though each interval represents two responses.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A scaled graph's 6 intervals can represent 12 respondents.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Read the labeled scale and multiply intervals by the frequency per interval.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: A two-category OR comparison is treated as only one subtraction.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original question family can require combining two distinct categories before comparing with a third.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Add both separate category counts, then subtract the third count.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Fictional data are presented as the real class survey.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original lesson requires the genuine preceding survey.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Retain actual Lesson 6 survey data for source work; label sample graphs and numbers fictional.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Graph is missing a scale, axis labels or category names.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Frequency cannot be recovered or checked reliably.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Show clear graph title, category and frequency labels, and a consistent vertical scale.

SummaryPoints: Use the authentic collected prior-lesson data in a consistent scaled bar graph.
Select and label a sensible scale; verify maximum and minimum counts.
Ask and answer one-step how-many-more/fewer questions and two-step A-or-B-versus-C questions.
Exchange graphs and explain solutions; teacher assesses original open tasks.
Independent fictional numeric samples do not replace actual survey results; publisher-gated Cool-down and original figures are unverified.
